request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 46-year-old male with a history of MSA with predominant parkinsonism

Hospital Course:
The patient was emergently admitted to our neurological department with tracheal intubation due to sudden respiratory failure at night. He had a history of high-pitched snore at age 38 and neck and trunk rigidity, bradykinesia, postural tremor, and dysuria at age 44. He was diagnosed with MSA at age 45. The possibility of MSA-related central respiratory disorder or obstructive respiratory disorder due to MSA and/or obesity was considered after pulmonary inflammatory diseases were excluded. The patient underwent tracheostomy to maintain the airway after extubation which was successful, but continuous positive airway pressure may have also been helpful. Polysomnography showed obstructive SA, but not central SA. Awake fiberoptic laryngoscopy displayed no upper-airway obstruction but slight vocal-cord abduction impairment during inspiration while sleep laryngoscopy was refused by the patient. To assess the spatial and temporal conditions of the upper respiratory tract, including the nasal passages, pharynx, larynx, and portion of the trachea, 4D-CT during sleep was performed. The effective dose was 1.84 mSv.

Findings:
Reconstructed 4D-CT images of respiration during sleep revealed abnormal upper-airway findings compared with the images acquired during awake respiration: glottis closure at the terminal stage of inspiration, subsequent velopharyngeal closure, and succeeding glottis opening and expansion of pharyngeal pressure, but no other upper airway-obstruction findings.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Disposition:
The patient was discharged with tracheostoma retained which was determined to be indispensable, although central apnea after tracheostomy may cause sudden central origin-related death. The patient was followed up at 14 months postoperatively, and no further airway-related complications were reported.

Procedures:
Tracheostomy.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
CODE: G47

The episode was driven by obstructive sleep apnoea. Polysomnography showed obstructive rather than central apnoea, and 4D-CT during sleep showed dynamic glottic and velopharyngeal closure. The underlying cause is multiple system atrophy (G90.3), but the admission was for the airway obstruction, which is classified as sleep apnoea (G47.3) in the nervous system chapter. The respiratory failure was a consequence of that obstruction rather than a primary respiratory disease, and the discharge summary withholds its diagnosis section, so this is an inference from the course.
